blocks.text: PART 1. TESTOSTERONE AND hCG SAFETY INFORMATION
Last updated: November 19, 2026  |  Effective: November 19, 2026  |  Version 1.0
1. Emergency information

**Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room right away if you have any of these:**
•  Chest pain, pressure or tightness, or pain in your arm, neck, jaw or back.
•  Sudden shortness of breath, a fast heartbeat, or coughing up blood.
•  Signs of a stroke: face drooping, arm or leg weakness on one side, trouble speaking, sudden confusion, sudden trouble seeing, or a sudden severe headache.
•  Pain, swelling, warmth or redness in one leg, especially the calf.
•  A severe allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, or a widespread rash or hives.
•  An erection that lasts more than 4 hours.
Do not wait for a reply by email, chat, text message or the patient portal.
If you may have taken too much medicine, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Call 911 if the person collapses, has a seizure, has trouble breathing or cannot be woken up.
2. About this information

This page gives general safety information for adult men who are prescribed testosterone (by injection or as a cream) or human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) through WellPeps, a Wyoming corporation (“WellPeps”). Testosterone treats low testosterone (hypogonadism) when a clinician confirms it with blood tests and symptoms. This page does not replace your prescription label, your pharmacy’s paperwork, a Medication Guide or your clinician’s advice.

**WellPeps is not a medical practice or a pharmacy.** WellPeps helps you reach telehealth services provided by independent licensed clinicians of OSI Medical Services, P.A. (the “Practice”). WellPeps does not prescribe, compound or dispense medication.
**A licensed clinician decides** whether a prescription is medically appropriate for you, after reviewing your symptoms, health history and lab results. A prescription is not guaranteed.

**A state-licensed pharmacy** prepares and ships your medication. Your label names it. Pharmacies that fill WellPeps prescriptions: OSI / Scriptful Rx, 433 Plaza Real, Suite 275, Boca Raton, FL 33432.
**Your label comes first.** If this page and your label disagree, follow your label and contact your clinician or pharmacy.
3. About your medicine

**Testosterone injection and testosterone cream are compounded.** A compounded medicine is made by a state-licensed pharmacy for you, based on your prescriber’s order. Your label and pharmacy paperwork tell you what you have.
**Compounded medicines are not FDA-approved.** FDA does not review them for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.

A compounded medicine is not the same as, equivalent to or interchangeable with an FDA-approved product, even when the active ingredient has the same name. The strength, form and how fast it is absorbed can be different.

**hCG** is a manufactured prescription medicine, not compounded. It is sometimes prescribed with testosterone to help maintain natural testosterone production or fertility. hCG is not approved for weight loss and should not be used for it.
Every warning on this page applies to your medicine. See also the Compounded Medication Disclosure and Consent.
4. Testosterone is a controlled substance
Testosterone is a Schedule III controlled substance under federal law. It can be misused, and using more than prescribed can cause serious harm.
**Use only your own prescription, only as directed.** It is illegal to sell or give your testosterone to anyone else.
Keep it in a secure place, out of reach of children, and keep track of how much you have.

Taking higher doses than prescribed, or stopping suddenly after long use at high doses, can cause problems including mood changes, depression and withdrawal symptoms. Tell your clinician if you feel you need more than prescribed.
5. Do not use testosterone if you
Have, or may have, breast cancer or prostate cancer.
Are a woman who is pregnant, may become pregnant or is breastfeeding. Testosterone can harm an unborn baby.
Are allergic to testosterone or to any ingredient in your medicine, including the oil in an injection (for example, cottonseed oil) or the cream base. Ask the pharmacy for the full ingredient list.

**Tell your clinician before you start if you have** heart disease, high blood pressure, a past heart attack or stroke, blood clots, a high red blood cell count, sleep apnea, an enlarged prostate or trouble urinating, liver or kidney disease, diabetes, high cholesterol, swelling in your legs or ankles, depression or another mental health condition, or if you are trying to have children. Tell them every medicine and supplement you take, especially blood thinners, insulin or diabetes medicines, and corticosteroids.
6. Key warning for testosterone cream: protect others from contact

**Testosterone on your skin can pass to other people.** Children and women who touch the area where you applied the cream, or clothing or towels that touched it, can absorb testosterone. In children this can cause early puberty signs (such as enlarged genitals, early pubic hair, aggressive behavior). In women it can cause acne and unwanted hair growth, and it can harm an unborn baby.
Wash your hands with soap and water right after applying the cream.
Let the cream dry, then cover the area with clothing. Keep it covered until you wash it off.
Wash the application area with soap and water before any skin-to-skin contact with another person.
If someone touches the area, they should wash their skin with soap and water right away. Tell your clinician if a child or woman shows the signs above.
Apply only where your label says. Do not apply to the genitals unless your clinician tells you to.
7. Serious risks and the tests that watch for them
Your clinician will order blood tests before you start and regularly during treatment. Keep these appointments. Lab tests are billed separately.

Thickens the blood and can raise the risk of blood clots, heart attack and stroke. More common with injections.

Clots in the legs or lungs have been reported. See Emergency information for warning signs.

Testosterone can raise blood pressure, which raises the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Studies on heart risk have had mixed results. Some men had more irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation).

Testosterone can make an enlarged prostate worse and may speed the growth of an existing prostate cancer.

Testosterone lowers sperm production and can cause infertility, sometimes for a long time.

Can start or get worse, especially if you are overweight.
Snoring, pauses in breathing, daytime sleepiness

Swelling in ankles or legs, sometimes serious in people with heart, kidney or liver disease.

blocks.text: 8. Stop and contact your clinician if you have
Trouble urinating, a weak stream, or needing to urinate often, especially at night.
Breast swelling or tenderness.
Swelling of the ankles, feet or legs, or fast weight gain.
Snoring that is new or worse, or pauses in breathing during sleep.
Mood changes, new or worse depression, aggression or thoughts of harming yourself. If you are thinking about harming yourself, call or text 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) or 911.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain in the upper right belly.
Erections that happen too often or last too long.
9. hCG: what is different
hCG is given by injection under the skin or into a muscle, on a schedule set by your clinician.
Possible side effects include headache, tiredness, mood changes, irritability, breast tenderness or swelling, fluid retention and pain at the injection site.
Do not use hCG if you have, or may have, prostate cancer or another hormone-sensitive cancer, or if you are allergic to it.
Rarely, hCG can cause serious allergic reactions or blood clots. See Emergency information.
10. Other possible side effects

Common side effects of testosterone include acne or oily skin, pain, redness or a lump where you inject or apply it, changes in mood or sex drive, hair loss or more body hair, headache and changes in lab results. Tell your clinician if a side effect bothers you or does not go away.
11. Using your medicine safely
Use exactly the dose and schedule on your label. Do not change your dose or stop without talking to your clinician.

**Injections:** use a new sterile needle and syringe every time, never share needles or vials, and inject only where you were shown. Dispose of needles in a sharps container. Some people cough or feel short of breath right after an oil injection; if this is severe or does not pass quickly, call 911.
**Cream:** apply to clean, dry, unbroken skin where your label says, at the same time each day. Do not apply more often than prescribed.
If you miss a dose, follow your label or ask your clinician. Do not double up.
Tell any other doctor, dentist or emergency team that you use testosterone or hCG, and before any surgery.
12. Storage and product quality
Follow the storage directions on your label or in your pharmacy paperwork. Keep injections at room temperature unless your label says otherwise, and protect them from light.
Keep your medicine and supplies out of reach of children and pets, in a secure place.

Do not use your medicine if the package is damaged or opened, the label is missing or unclear, the liquid looks cloudy or has particles when it should be clear, it looks or smells different from your last fill, or it is past the date on the label. Call the pharmacy first.
If your package arrives late or was left in heat or cold, contact the pharmacy before you use it. See also the Shipping and Delivery Policy.
13. Questions and reporting problems
**Non-emergency medical questions:** message your clinician in the patient portal at portal.wellpeps.com.
**Orders, shipping or billing help:** support@wellpeps.com or (307) 881-8700, during normal business hours. WellPeps support cannot answer medical questions.
**Ingredients, strength, preparation, storage or the date on the label:** the pharmacy named on your label.
**To report a side effect or product problem to FDA:** MedWatch at www.fda.gov/medwatch or 1-800-FDA-1088. Please also tell your clinician.
14. This is not everything

This page is a summary. It does not list every warning, side effect or interaction. If your prescription label, your pharmacy’s paperwork, a Medication Guide or your clinician’s instructions disagree with this page, follow them and ask your clinician or pharmacy. Read the paperwork that comes with each fill.
